metadata.title: ERISA Litigation Case Research - COLA II Pattern Validation
metadata.purpose: Document actual lawsuit patterns that COLA II detection engine is trained on

cases.court: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Missouri

key_violations.description: Fidelity received 12b-1 fees and revenue sharing from mutual funds without adequate disclosure to participants
key_violations.court_language: The Court finds that Fidelity's receipt of revenue sharing payments constituted an impermissible use of plan assets

key_violations.description: Fidelity retained float income from uninvested contributions during settlement periods without crediting the plan
key_violations.court_language: Fidelity improperly retained float income earned during settlement periods rather than crediting it to participant accounts

key_violations.description: Plan offered retail Class A shares when lower-cost institutional shares were available
key_violations.court_language: ABB breached its fiduciary duty by failing to offer the lowest-cost share class available to the Plan

key_violations.description: Plan fees used to subsidize non-plan corporate services including health & welfare plan administration
key_violations.court_language: The use of plan assets to pay for corporate services violated ERISA's prohibited transaction rules

key_findings: Fidelity acted as both service provider and fund affiliate - inherent conflict
Revenue sharing arrangements were not clearly disclosed in service agreements
Float income procedures not disclosed to plan fiduciaries
Recordkeeping fees used cross-subsidy model rather than explicit per-participant pricing
public_documents: Expert testimony on revenue sharing practices
cases.cola_detection_notes: COLA II patterns directly match language from court findings. Revenue sharing and float income are primary targets.

key_violations.description: Recordkeeping fees exceeded $350 per participant annually, well above industry averages
key_violations.court_language: The Second Circuit found that fees exceeding $350 per participant raised material issues of fact about whether fiduciaries adequately monitored costs

key_violations.description: Plan fiduciaries failed to benchmark recordkeeping fees against comparable plans
key_violations.court_language: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged that defendants failed to conduct adequate market checks or fee benchmarking

key_findings: Supreme Court ruling (2024) lowered pleading standard for excessive fee claims
Mere fact of high fees compared to market is sufficient to state a claim
$350/participant became de facto benchmark threshold for raising red flags
Plan size matters - larger plans should negotiate better rates
cases.cola_detection_notes: COLA II flags fees >$350/participant based on this precedent. Absence of benchmarking language also triggers warnings.

cases.court: U.S. District Court, Central District of California

key_violations.description: Plan offered proprietary Amgen-affiliated funds without adequate disclosure of conflicts of interest
key_violations.court_language: Defendants failed to adequately disclose the conflicts of interest inherent in offering affiliated investment products

key_violations.description: Revenue sharing arrangements between Fidelity and fund providers not clearly disclosed
key_violations.court_language: The disclosure failed to provide participants with meaningful information about revenue sharing affecting their investments

key_findings: Affiliate relationships create inherent conflicts that must be disclosed
Generic disclosure language is insufficient - specifics required
Revenue sharing affecting fund lineups must be transparent
Participants must be able to assess whether conflicts influenced fund selection
cases.cola_detection_notes: COLA II specifically looks for affiliate language without accompanying conflict disclosures.

cases.court: U.S. District Court, Northern District of Illinois

key_violations.description: Fee disclosures referred to 'other agreements' and 'separate documents' without providing them
key_violations.court_language: Disclosure stated compensation details could be found in 'other agreements' but failed to provide those agreements or sufficient detail

key_violations.description: Multiple service providers and tiered fee structures made actual costs impossible for participants to determine
key_violations.court_language: The complexity of the fee structure itself violated the duty to provide clear, understandable information

key_findings: Simply providing document titles is insufficient - actual information required
Complexity can itself violate disclosure obligations
Participants should not need advanced degrees to understand fees
Referring to other documents creates scavenger hunt - prohibited
cases.cola_detection_notes: COLA II counts 'refer elsewhere' instances and flags when threshold exceeded (5+ instances).

detection_validation.validation_method: Synthetic test cases matching court language

revenue_sharing_presence.description: Any undisclosed revenue sharing is critical

demo_talking_points: Every pattern in COLA II maps to actual litigation outcomes
Tussey v. ABB: $55M judgment validates our revenue sharing detection
Cornell Supreme Court case: Our $350 threshold is now legal precedent
Harris v. Amgen: $30M proves affiliate disclosure matters
Combined settlement value: $90M+ from patterns we detect automatically

obtaining_test_documents.note: Actual litigation PDFs require PACER access (~$20 total)
obtaining_test_documents.recommended_for_demo: Use provider sample disclosures + synthetic test cases
